## &nbsp; {.dark .mid background-color="#1C242B"}

:::: {.vcenter}
::: {.statement}
A research paper is not a report<br>of what you did.
:::

::: {.statement-hi}
It is an argument that a claim<br>is warranted by evidence.
:::

::: {.note}
Everything in the next thirteen weeks follows from this one sentence.
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
**[00:06 – 00:09] · THE THESIS OF THE COURSE**

**SAY —**

"Before anything else, one sentence.

A research paper is not a report of what you did."

*[ pause three or four seconds — do not fill it ]*

"It is an argument that a claim is warranted by evidence.

Those two sound similar. They are not. A report answers the question 'what did I do?' An argument answers a different question: 'what do I claim, and why should you believe me?'

Almost every problem I see in student writing comes from answering the first question when the reader is asking the second.

Everything in the next thirteen weeks follows from this one sentence. Why the gap sits where it sits. Why Methods is written in the past tense. Why the Discussion hedges. All of it comes from here."

**DO —** Return to this slide in the Activity 1 debrief, and again in Week 15.
:::

## The work is not finished when the data are in

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
Why this course exists
:::

::: {.cards}
::: {.card .c-rust}
[]{.dot}

### Unread

A result nobody can follow does not enter the record. It is, functionally, not a result.
:::

::: {.card .c-amber}
[]{.dot}

### Unfunded

Proposals, reports, and theses are all the same skill under different constraints.
:::

::: {.card .c-teal}
[]{.dot}

### Unhired

Your writing is the only part of your work most people will ever see.
:::
:::

::: {.foot}
::: {.note}
This course treats writing as a designed object — something with a structure you can inspect, test, and repair.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
**[00:09 – 00:12] · WHY THIS COURSE EXISTS**

**SAY —**

"Three reasons this course exists.

First: a result nobody can follow does not enter the record. I am not claiming good work is never found. I am saying it is found late, and by fewer people.

Second — and this is the honest one — every proposal you write, every progress report, every thesis chapter, is this same skill under a different word limit. You will do this for the rest of your career whether or not you stay in a university.

Third: for most of the people who will ever judge your work — a reviewer, a funding panel, a hiring committee — your writing is your work. They never see the laboratory.

So in this course we treat writing as a designed object. Something with a structure you can inspect, test, and repair. Not a talent you either have or you do not."

**DO —** Go straight into Activity 1. Do not take questions here; there is nothing yet to ask about.
:::

## Take it apart, then build one {.tint background-color="#F3F0EB"}

::: {.kicker .c-teal}
How the course is built
:::

::: {.cards .feature}
::: {.card .c-teal}
[Part I · Weeks 1–6]{.eyebrow}

### Analysis

You reverse-engineer published papers. You write nothing of your own. You learn to see structure.
:::

::: {.card .c-amber}
[Part II · Weeks 7–14]{.eyebrow}

### Design

You build one manuscript of your own, section by section, in the same order you learned to take one apart.
:::
:::

::: {.foot}
::: {.note}
Every session in Part I sets the criteria that the matching session in Part II asks you to satisfy.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
**[ optional — fold into the Debrief 2 bridge if you are behind ] · HOW THE COURSE IS BUILT**

**SAY —**

"One more thing about the structure, and then we start.

The catalogue description says this course has two parts: analysis, and design.

Weeks one to six, you take other people's papers apart. You write nothing of your own.

Weeks seven to fourteen, you build one manuscript, section by section, in the same order you learned to take one apart.

Every session in the first half sets the standard that the matching session in the second half asks you to meet. That is the whole design."

**DO —** This split has been in the catalogue for years. 2026 is the first year the weekly plan actually enacts it.
:::

## The 60-second research pitch {.dark .divider .c-amber background-color="#1C242B"}

::: {.kicker}
Activity 1 · 15 minutes
:::

::: {.lede}
Everyone speaks. Exactly sixty seconds.<br>
The clock is on screen and I will cut you off.
:::

::: {.note}
This is your introduction — and it is also the first thing this course measures.
:::

::: {.notes}
**[00:12] · ACTIVITY 1 — LAUNCH**

**SAY —**

"Right. Here is what we are doing.

Each of you speaks for exactly sixty seconds. The clock is on the screen. When it reaches zero I will stop you, even in the middle of a sentence.

This is your introduction to the class. It is also the first thing this course measures."

**DO —** CRITICAL: do not teach the six genres before this. The whole diagnostic value depends on them attempting a gap statement with no vocabulary to hide behind. Do not take questions about the format either — the ambiguity is part of it.
:::

## Four sentences. No more.

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
Activity 1
:::

::: {.numbered .n4}
1. **Who** I am \_\_\_, and I work on \_\_\_.
2. **The problem** The difficulty in this area is that \_\_\_.
3. **The attempt** What I am trying to do about it is \_\_\_.
4. **Why it matters** If it works, \_\_\_ becomes possible.
:::

::: {.foot}
::: {.note}
Sentence 2 is the one most people cannot finish. Notice that while you listen.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
**[00:12 – 00:27] · ACTIVITY 1 — RUN**

**SAY —**

"Four sentences, in this order.

One: who you are, and what you work on.

Two: the problem — what is difficult or unresolved in that area.

Three: what you are trying to do about it.

Four: why it matters — what becomes possible if it works.

Take two minutes to write them down. Then we go round the room in seating order, starting here.

One warning before you begin. Sentence two is the hard one. Watch what happens to it."

**DO —**

- Two minutes of writing, then about twelve minutes of pitches.
- Seating order, not volunteers — confident students set an unreachable standard if they go first.
- Enforce the cut-off from student number one. Uncomfortable once, instructive for the term.
- PRIVATE RECORD: how many reach sentence 3 before the timer stops. That is the cohort baseline; compare it against the Week 15 presentations. It is usually under half.
- Cohort above 14: split into two parallel rows, and take report-outs from three volunteers only.
:::

## You are not an audience. You are reviewers. {.tint background-color="#F3F0EB"}

::: {.kicker .c-teal}
While you listen
:::

::: {.cards}
::: {.card .c-teal}
**Pick any two classmates. For each of them, write down:**

- Could you state their **gap** in one sentence?
- Could you state what they will **actually do**?
- Mark each: yes / no / almost
:::
:::

::: {.foot}
::: {.flag}
Keep the slip. We will look at it again in Week 15.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
**[ display alongside the pitch template while the pitches run ] · THE LISTENING TASK**

**SAY —**

"While your classmates are speaking, you have a job.

Pick any two of them. For each one write down two things. Could you state their gap in one sentence? And could you state what they are actually going to do? Mark each one yes, almost, or no.

You are not judging them. You are finding out how hard it is to pull a gap out of somebody else's words — which is exactly what a reader does with your Introduction.

Keep that slip. We will look at it again in Week 15."

**DO —** Collect nothing. The experience is the point, not the data.
:::

## What just happened

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
Debrief
:::

::: {.dots}
- **Sentence 1 was easy** Everyone can say what they work on. Topic is not the same as contribution.
- **Sentence 2 was hard** Most gap statements came out as "not much work has been done on X." That is an absence, not a gap.
- **Sentence 3 drifted** Several of you described methods instead of an aim. Method is how; aim is what you will settle.
- **Sentence 4 disappeared** The significance often vanished under the time limit — exactly as it vanishes under a word limit.
:::

::: {.foot}
::: {.note}
Weeks 5 and 7 are about sentence 2. Week 10 is about sentence 4.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
**[00:27 – 00:42] · DEBRIEF 1**

**SAY —**

"Let us look at what just happened.

Sentence one was easy. Everybody can say what they work on. But notice — that is your topic, not your contribution. Nobody funds a topic.

Sentence two was hard. Most of you said something close to 'not much work has been done on this.' That is an absence, not a gap. An absence is a fact about the literature. A gap is a claim about why that absence matters — what we cannot currently do, or predict, or explain, because of it. Learning to tell those two apart is most of Weeks five and seven.

Sentence three drifted. Several of you described your methods instead of your aim. Method is how. Aim is what you will settle.

And sentence four often disappeared altogether — the timer ate it. That is exactly what a word limit does to significance. Week ten is about protecting it."

**DO —** Adapt all four to what actually happened. If the cohort did well on sentence 2, say so — then ask them to write their sentence down and compare it in Week 7.
:::

## Seven gates between your bench and a citation

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
The journey
:::

::: {.steps}
::: {.step .c-teal}
[1]{.n}[Result]{.h}[in your notebook]{.d}
:::
::: {.step .c-teal}
[2]{.n}[Claim]{.h}[one sentence]{.d}
:::
::: {.step .c-teal}
[3]{.n}[Manuscript]{.h}[the argument]{.d}
:::
::: {.step .c-amber}
[4]{.n}[Desk]{.h}[editor screens]{.d}
:::
::: {.step .c-amber}
[5]{.n}[Review]{.h}[2–3 referees]{.d}
:::
::: {.step .c-amber}
[6]{.n}[Revision]{.h}[and response]{.d}
:::
::: {.step .c-plum}
[7]{.n}[Record]{.h}[cited, or not]{.d}
:::
:::

::: {.lede}
Weeks 12 and 13 bring in editors who work gates 4 to 6 for a living.
:::

::: {.foot}
::: {.punch}
Most manuscripts die at gate 4, before a single referee reads them. Nothing about that gate is about your science.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
**[00:42 – 00:52] · SEVEN GATES**

**SAY —**

"Seven gates between your bench and a citation.

One, two and three are yours alone. You have a result. You turn it into a claim. You build a manuscript around that claim.

Four, five and six belong to other people. An editor screens it. Two or three referees read it. You revise, and you respond.

Seven belongs to the field. Somebody cites it, or nobody does.

Now — here is the part I want you to remember.

Most manuscripts die at gate four. Before a single referee reads them. And nothing about that gate is a judgement on your science. A desk rejection is a decision about scope and framing: is this paper for this journal's readers, and is it worth three referees' time?

I say this now because the first time it happens to you it will feel like a verdict on your work. It is not. Weeks twelve and thirteen bring in two editors who make that decision for a living, and you can ask them yourselves."

**DO —** Slow down on the rust-coloured line. It is the sentence they take home.
:::

## You are never writing for one audience {.tint background-color="#F3F0EB"}

::: {.kicker .c-teal}
Four readers
:::

::: {.cards}
::: {.card .c-amber}
[~3 minutes]{.chip}

### Editor

Is this in scope, and is it worth three referees' time?
:::

::: {.card .c-teal}
[~2 hours]{.chip}

### Referee

Do the methods support the claim?
:::

::: {.card .c-sky}
[~40 seconds]{.chip}

### Skimmer

Title, abstract, figures. Then leave or stay.
:::

::: {.card .c-sage}
[~a week]{.chip}

### Builder

Can I reproduce this and build on it?
:::
:::

::: {.foot}
::: {.note}
The abstract is read by all four. That is why Week 11 spends three hours on it.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
**[00:52 – 01:00] · FOUR READERS**

**SAY —**

"Four readers, four completely different attention budgets.

The editor gives you about three minutes. The referee gives you about two hours. The skimmer gives you forty seconds — title, abstract, figures, and then they leave or they stay. The builder gives you a week, because they are trying to reproduce what you did.

Question for the room. Which of these four reads the abstract?"

*[ wait for the answer — do not supply it ]*

"All of them. Every single one. That is why Week eleven spends three hours on two hundred words."

**DO —** Actually wait. If you are running behind, cut the Builder card and keep the other three.
:::

## Six genres {.dark .divider .c-amber background-color="#1C242B"}

::: {.kicker}
Block 3 · 35 minutes
:::

::: {.lede}
Same findings. Six different documents.<br>The difference is not style — it is purpose.
:::

::: {.notes}
**[01:10] · SECTION DIVIDER**

**SAY —**

"Same findings. Six different documents. The difference between them is not style — it is purpose. That is the next half hour."

## What each one is for

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
The six
:::

::: {.cards .g3}
::: {.card .c-teal}
[]{.dot}

### Research paper

A new claim, with the evidence that warrants it
:::

::: {.card .c-rust}
[]{.dot}

### Communication

A result too urgent to wait for the full study
:::

::: {.card .c-sky}
[]{.dot}

### Review

A map of what a field currently believes
:::

::: {.card .c-sage}
[]{.dot}

### Data paper

A dataset described so others can reuse it
:::

::: {.card .c-plum}
[]{.dot}

### Technical report

An account for a client or an institution
:::

::: {.card .c-amber}
[]{.dot}

### Thesis

A demonstration that you can do research
:::
:::

::: {.foot}
::: {.note}
Choosing the wrong genre is the most expensive mistake in this list — it wastes months before anyone reads a word.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
**[01:10 – 01:18] · THE SIX GENRES**

**SAY —**

"Six genres. One line each for now — the detail comes next.

Research paper: a new claim, with the evidence that warrants it.

Communication, or Letter: a result too urgent to wait for the full study.

Review: a map of what a field currently believes.

Data paper: a dataset described so that somebody else can reuse it.

Technical report: an account written for a client or an institution.

Thesis: a demonstration that you can do research.

Now — the expensive mistake on this list is not writing badly. It is choosing the wrong genre. That wastes months before anybody reads a word.

Has anyone here already been told to turn something into a communication?"

**DO —** Take one or two stories if they come. A student's own account lands harder than yours.
:::

## You can tell the genre without reading the science {.tint background-color="#F3F0EB"}

::: {.kicker .c-teal}
Structural evidence
:::

::: {.evidence}
|   |   |
|---|---|
| Length | 2 500 words says Communication. 14 000 says Review. Nothing else is close. |
| Reference count | Under 40 means original work. Over 150 is almost certainly a Review. |
| Section headings | IMRaD means an argument. Thematic headings mean a survey. |
| Methods section | Absent, or in supplementary material? Communication. |
| Figure-to-word ratio | High and rising · Communication. Low · Review or report. |
| Front matter | Executive summary means an institutional reader, not a referee. |
:::

::: {.foot}
::: {.note}
This is the skill Activity 2 asks you to use. It is also the whole of Week 4.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
**[01:18 – 01:24] · STRUCTURAL EVIDENCE**

**SAY —**

"Here is how you tell them apart without reading the science.

Length. Two and a half thousand words says Communication. Fourteen thousand says Review. Nothing else is close.

Reference count. Under forty means original work. Over a hundred and fifty is almost certainly a review.

Section headings. IMRaD means an argument. Thematic headings mean a survey.

The Methods section. If it is missing from the body — pushed into supplementary material — that is a Communication. Remember that one.

Figure-to-word ratio. High means Communication. Low means review or report.

Front matter. An executive summary means the reader may stop there. No referee ever stops there.

These are evidence, not rules. Evidence can conflict. In a few minutes you will find out what happens when it does."

**DO —** Do not hint at which dossier is the ambiguous one.
:::

## The research paper

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
Genre 1
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}
- **Makes ONE claim.**
- Everything else in the paper exists to warrant that claim.
- IMRaD is not a template — it is the shape of an argument: here is the question, here is how I answered it, here is what I found, here is what it means.
- The Methods section is a promise of reproducibility. It is what separates this genre from journalism.
:::

::: {.column width="42%"}
::: {.spec}
[Typical shape]{.eyebrow}

Words
:   6 000 – 9 000

Figures
:   5 – 8

References
:   40 – 80

Review time
:   3 – 9 months

Headings
:   IMRaD
:::
:::
::::

::: {.foot}
::: {.flag}
Weeks 5–11 build one of these, section by section.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
**[01:24 – 01:30] · THE RESEARCH PAPER**

**SAY —**

"This is the one you will write.

A research paper makes one claim. One. Everything else in the document exists to warrant it.

And IMRaD is not a template you fill in. It is the shape of an argument. Here is the question. Here is how I answered it. Here is what I found. Here is what it means. The same four moves as your sixty-second pitch, at twenty times the length.

The Methods section is a promise — a promise that somebody else could do this again and get what you got. That promise is what separates this genre from journalism.

The panel on the right is for calibration only. Do not memorise the numbers. Notice the proportions: enough method to replicate, enough references to situate, and not enough to survey."
:::

## Two opposite answers to "how much?"

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
Genres 2 and 3
:::

::: {.cards .feature}
::: {.card .c-rust}
[]{.dot}

### Communication

- Speed is the argument — you are claiming this cannot wait
- Methods usually pushed to supplementary
- One figure carries the whole claim
- Rejected hardest for lack of novelty
:::

::: {.card .c-sky}
[]{.dot}

### Review

- Synthesis is the argument — a new way to organise what is known
- A list of papers is not a review; it is a bibliography
- Thematic headings, not IMRaD
- Usually invited — check before you write one
:::
:::

::: {.foot}
::: {.note}
Both are "a paper." Neither can be written the way you would write the other.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
**[01:30 – 01:37] · COMMUNICATION AND REVIEW**

**SAY —**

"Two opposite answers to the question 'how much?'

A Communication argues by speed. You are claiming this cannot wait. Which is exactly why they are rejected hardest for lack of novelty — if it could have waited, it should have. Methods go to supplementary. Usually one figure carries the entire claim.

A Review argues by synthesis. And this is where people go wrong: a list of papers is not a review, it is a bibliography. A review earns its place by reorganising a field — by proposing an order that was not obvious before.

One practical warning. Most reviews in our field are invited. Check before you spend three months writing one."

**DO —** If time is short, cut the Review half to a single sentence.
:::

## The three you will also write {.tint background-color="#F3F0EB"}

::: {.kicker .c-teal}
Genres 4, 5 and 6
:::

::: {.cards .stack}
::: {.card .c-sage}
[]{.dot}

### Data paper

The dataset is the contribution. No hypothesis is required — but the description must be complete enough for someone else to reuse it without asking you a question.
:::

::: {.card .c-plum}
[]{.dot}

### Technical report

Written for a client or an institution, not for referees. Executive summary first, because the reader may stop there. Not peer reviewed, and not part of the permanent record.
:::

::: {.card .c-amber}
[]{.dot}

### Thesis

Its purpose is not to report findings but to demonstrate that you can do research. That is why it contains material a journal would cut — failed attempts, full derivations, the reasoning behind choices.
:::
:::

::: {.foot}
::: {.note}
Your thesis is not a stack of papers, and your papers are not chapters. Converting between them is real work.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
**[01:37 – 01:45] · THE OTHER THREE**

**SAY —**

"Three more, and you will write all of them at some point.

Data paper: the dataset is the contribution. No hypothesis required. But the description has to be complete enough that a stranger can reuse it without sending you an email.

Technical report: written for a client or an institution, not for referees. Executive summary first, because your reader may stop there. Not peer reviewed, and not part of the permanent record.

And the thesis. Its purpose is not to report findings. Its purpose is to demonstrate that you can do research. That is exactly why it contains everything a journal would cut — the attempts that failed, the full derivations, the reasoning behind your choices.

Which brings me to something several of you are about to discover. Your thesis is not a stack of papers, and your papers are not chapters. Converting between them is real work, and it is not copy and paste."
:::

## Six Papers, Six Purposes {.dark .divider .c-teal background-color="#1C242B"}

::: {.kicker}
Activity 2 · 15 minutes · in pairs
:::

::: {.lede}
Six dossiers. Titles, three lines of abstract, headings, counts.<br>
The journal name has been removed.
:::

::: {.flag}
Work out what each one is — from its shape alone.
:::

::: {.notes}
**[01:45] · ACTIVITY 2 — LAUNCH**

**SAY —**

"Now you try it.

On your table are six dossiers. Each one shows a title, three lines of an abstract, some counts, and the list of section headings. The journal name has been removed.

Work in pairs. Seven minutes. Work out what each one is — from its shape alone."

**DO —** Hand out the sets now if they are not already down. Start the clock and say you will call time.
:::

## What to do

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
Activity 2
:::

::: {.numbered .n3}
1. **7 min · in pairs** For each of the six dossiers, write down three things.
2. **8 min · report out** We take them in order. Number 6 last.
:::

::: {.cards}
::: {.card .c-amber}
**For each dossier, record:**

1. Which genre is it?
2. The two strongest structural clues
3. Who is the intended reader?
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
**[01:45 – 02:00] · ACTIVITY 2 — RUN AND REPORT**

**SAY —**

"For each dossier write down three things. Which genre it is. The two strongest structural clues you used. And who the intended reader is.

Seven minutes. Go."

*[ after seven minutes ]*

"Right, let us take them. A, B, C, D, E — and we will do number six last."

**DO —**

- Circulate during the pairs phase and listen for which dossier is causing argument. It is usually F.
- ANSWER KEY: A research paper · B communication · C review · D data paper · E technical report · F COMMUNICATION.
- Take A to E quickly. Take F last and deliberately, and let the disagreement run two or three minutes before resolving it.
- If nobody finds it, ask: "If you wanted to repeat this experiment, where would you go to find the method?" The decisive clue in F is not the length — it is that the Methods are in Supporting Information, exactly as in B.
:::

## How credit actually works

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
Block 5
:::

::: {.dots}
- **Authorship is earned, not granted** Contribution to design, execution, or interpretation — plus drafting, plus approval, plus accountability. Supervising a project is not automatically one of them.
- **Order carries meaning — and it varies** First author did the work; last author ran the group. In some fields. Never assume; ask before the first draft, not after.
- **Citation is the currency** It is also the audit trail. An uncited idea that is not yours is misconduct, whatever the intention.
- **The record is permanent** Retractions stay visible. So does everything you sign your name to.
:::

::: {.foot}
::: {.note}
Next week Prof. Supareak takes this apart in full — ICMJE criteria, COPE guidance, and the course AI policy.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
**[02:25 – 02:35] · HOW CREDIT WORKS**

**SAY —**

"Four things nobody tells a first-year graduate student.

One. Authorship is earned against criteria, not granted by seniority. Contribution to design, execution or interpretation — plus drafting or critical revision, plus approval, plus accountability. Supervising a project is not automatically any of those.

Two. Author order carries meaning, and the meaning varies by field and by country. In our field, first did the work and last ran the group. That is not universal. So never assume — ask, in writing, before the first draft. Not after. After, the incentives have changed and nobody can back down gracefully.

Three. Citation is the currency, and it is also the audit trail. An idea that is not yours and is not cited is misconduct, whatever you intended.

Four. The record is permanent. Retractions stay visible forever. So does everything you put your name on.

That is as far as I go today. Professor Supareak takes the whole of next week on this — the formal criteria, the publisher guidance, and the course policy."

**DO —** Press points one and two. Do not go deeper; Week 2 covers ICMJE and COPE properly.
:::
